articleTitle: Metrology and process control: how process control can assist in calibrating the production line
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: This paper is an attempt to put into a few words a process that has taken a long time to prove and put into practice and is still being proven as time goes on. The goal of high product quality should be a never ending process, almost by definition, and in todays world of affordable high precision in is ever more important to keep on top of the production process to ensure the final product meets the design goals. The subject of this paper is the calibrating of the highest precision multifunction calibrator and the challenge of supporting its' accuracy and proving of the process by which it is being done, together with a look at a similar process verifying an essentially manual device, a precision AC/DC transfer device.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Designing for improved performance and reduced calibration costs
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: Instrument manufacturers have a considerable responsibility to their customers, because an inaccurate calibration can lead to claims for consequential loss as well as a damaged reputation. The manufacturer is of course aware of this responsibility, and will ensure that the instrument is correctly calibrated when it leaves the factory. The calibration and testing performed will be extensive, and cover all of the parameters specified in the manufacturer's technical literature for the product. In order to give products access to the widest possible market, instrument manufacturers provide more and more functionality in the instruments they produce. It is in the manufacturer's interest to ensure that the functionality of the instrument covers as many applications as possible. It follows then that such wide functionality must be fully tested and calibrated. However, the customer's application may utilize only a fraction of the instrument's capabilities. Careful consideration must be given to the test requirements in order to satisfy the customer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Product quality through accredited industrial calibration: a Spanish experience
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: In recent years quality has become a factor that increasingly governs the competitiveness of companies in global and interdependent markets. This is due to the fact that it provides double confidence: on the one hand to the clients and consumers, assuring them that the company works with a process that guarantees the quality of the product or service, and on the other, to the company itself, as it introduces an ordered and controlled system of organisation which ensures increased efficiency. Based on European directives, Spanish policy as regards industrial quality is focussed on promoting and supporting Spanish Industry in the efficient implementation of its quality systems in order that it may have easy access to recognised certification in the regulatory as well as voluntary domain.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The evolution of quality control standards for calibration systems over the past thirty years
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: The foresight of the authors of the early quality standards and their acceptance by UK Industry has established the UK as a world leader in the registration of Companies to ISO 9000 and accreditation of laboratories to EN 45001. The evolution of quality standards for calibration systems has given an important impetus and status to the field of metrology which in turn has greatly strengthened the standing of the UK National Measurement System and those working in it.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: This paper looks at ISO 9000 quality management systems requirements from the perspective of a calibration department providing an internal service to a company seeking registration. Each clause of ISO 9001-1987-is studied, concentrating on internal interfaces with other parts of the company seeking registration.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: The minimum content of a NAMAS calibration certificate is defined in NAMAS document M25 Certificates of Calibration, and all accredited laboratories are expected to comply with this. There does, however, remain the question of exactly what scope of calibration should be carried out. This is partly a matter for the contractual arrangements between the laboratory and the client. However many clients are not always aware of what their requirements are and therefore ask for a calibration to 'manufacturer's specification', and rely on advice from the calibration laboratory. This can give rise to all sorts of problems. The author therefore explores these problems with a view to moving this issue further forward so that mutually acceptable solutions can be explored.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Using template NAMAS procedures to provide quality calibration
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: Hewlett-Packard has service-centre wide NAMAS accreditation using metrology support packages (MSPs) which define measurements and uncertainties for each test on each instrument, for both Hewlett-Packard and other vendors' equipment. Although worthwhile for serial-to-serial and year-to-year consistency, an MSP can take a significant time to produce for which, one way or another, the customer has to pay. This paper describes some methods employed to address these issues.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improving and maintaining calibration: integrity in a cost conscious environment
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: As the electronics market place continues to expand into new and larger fields the need for periodic calibration increases by a similar amount. Unfortunately calibration is often viewed as an activity demanded only by quality system assessors resulting in very limited resources being made available to perform the function. This paper looks at two methods which have been employed to reduce the calibration overhead whilst at the same time maintaining similar levels of integrity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: A service organization operating through its calibration or testing laboratory as an issuing authority for certificates of calibration or test reports must ensure that the information given on the certificate or report is correct, traceable and that it is adequate for the customers purpose. The user of the certificate of calibration should ensure that the information and the measurements made on an instrument are what is required and that the uncertainties are acceptable. The user is advised to read calibration certificates carefully to make sure that they are of the correct type and to ensure the certificate meets their requirements. The user can greatly assist calibration laboratories by ensuring that the calibration requirements are discussed with the laboratory before the work is commenced. Finally, although 'time is of the essence' when calibration work is undertaken it should not be sacrificed at the expense of the quality of the results and due time must be allowed for the calibration work to be completed correctly.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The contribution of instrument calibration to product quality
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: All through the ages humanity has sought better value products with which to trade and improve the quality of life. The Craft Guilds and Liveried Companies were created to foster this ambition, and it was their success which generated trading companies who needed the support of governments who then in turn, became involved in fostering and regulating trade. In the UK, the NPL and BSI were established with suitable charters, controlled by Government via its trade ministry. There were parallel developments in other countries which inevitably led to bilateral and then multilateral trade agreements, the scene is thus set for highly organised competition in not only trade but product standards, safety standards and metrology. Competition for trade is thus not simply between manufacturing companies. Trade balances react on money exchange rates to which governments are very sensitive and will, in turn, react both overtly and covertly. Indeed, the management of trade and competition through the tools of national and international standards and trade agreements is now a major industry.<<ETX>>

articleTitle: The importance of traceability for the end user
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Contribution of Instrument Calibration to Product Quality
abstract: In this paper, the results of a small survey of manufacturing organisations are presented which gives some insight into their motives and knowledge in this area. The methodology developed was to survey manufacturing organisations which were known users of NAMAS accredited laboratories and to follow the derived benefits of traceable measurements up the traceability chain to the National Measurement Institute. The relevant part of the study for this paper focused on DC voltage and AC power.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
